notes.text: We have here the call by which Abram was removed out of the land of his nativity into the land of promise, which was designed both to try his faith and obedience, and also to set him apart for God. The circumstances of this call we may be somewhat helped to the knowledge of, from Stephen's speech, Acts vii, 2, where we are told, 1. That the God of glory appeared to him to give him this call, appeared in such displays of his glory as left Abram no room to doubt. God spake to him after in divers manners: but this first time, when the correspondence was to be settled, he appeared to him as the God of glory, and spake to him. 2. That this call was given him in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran, and in obedience to this call, he came out of the land of the Chaldeans, and dwelt in Charran or Haran about five years, and from thence, when his father was dead, by a fresh command, he removed him into the land of Canaan. Some think Haran was in Chaldea, and so was still a part of Abram's country; or he having staid there five years, began to call it his country, and to take root there, till God let him know this was not the place he was intended for. Get thee out of thy country — Now, (1.) By this precept he was tried whether he loved God better than he loved his native soil, and dearest friends, and whether he could willingly leave all to go along with God. His country was become idolatrous, his kindred and his father's house were a constant temptation to him, and he could not continue with them without danger of being infected by them; therefore get thee out, (Hebrew.) vade tibi, get thee gone with all speed, escape for thy life, look not behind thee. (2.) By this precept he was tried whether he could trust God farther than he saw him, for he must leave his own country to go to a land that God would shew him; he doth not say, 'tis a land that I will give thee nor doth he tell him what land it was, or what kind of land; but he must follow God with an implicit faith, and take God's word for it in the general, though he had no particular securities given him, that he should be no loser by leaving his country to follow God.

Here is added an encouraging promise, nay a complication of promises,

1. I will make of thee a great nation - When God took him from his own people, he promised to make him the head of another people. This promise was.

1. A great relief to Abram's burden, for he had now no child.

2. A great trial to Abram's faith, for his wife had been long barren, so that if he believe, it must be against hope, and his faith must build purely upon that power which can out of stones raise up children unto Abraham.

2. I will bless thee - Either particularly with the blessing of fruitfulness, as he had blessed Adam and Noah; or in general, I will bless thee with all manner of blessings, both of the upper and nether springs: leave thy father's house, and I will give thee a father's blessing, better than that of thy progenitors.
I will make thy name great — By deserting his country he lost his name there: care not for that, (saith God) but trust me, and I will make thee a greater name than ever thou couldst have had there.
Thou shalt be a blessing — That is, thy life shall be a blessing to the places where thou shalt sojourn.

I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee — This made it a kind of league offensive and defensive between God and Abram. Abram heartily espoused God's cause, and here God promiseth to interest himself in his.

In thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed — This was the promise that crowned all the rest, for it points at the Messiah, in whom all the promises are yea and amen.

4. So Abram departed - He was not disobedient to the heavenly vision. His obedience was speedy and without delay, submissive and without dispute.

5. They took with them the souls that they had gotten - That is, the proselytes they had made, and persuaded to worship the true God, and to go with them to Canaan; the souls which (as one of the Rabbins expresseth it) they had gathered under the wings of the divine Majesty.

6. The Canaanite was then in the land - He found the country possessed by Canaanites, who were likely to be but bad neighbours; and for ought appears he could not have ground to pitch his tent on but by their permission.

And the Lord appeared to Abram — Probably in a vision, and spoke to him comfortable words; Unto thy seed will I give this land - No place or condition can shut us out from God's gracious visits. Abram is a sojourner, unsettled, among Canaanites, and yet here also he meets with him that lives, and sees him. Enemies may part us and our tents, us and our altars, but not us and our God.

And there he built an altar unto the Lord who appeared to him, and called on the name of the Lord — Now consider this, (1.) As done upon a special occasion when God appeared to him, then and there he built an altar, with an eye to the God that appeared to him: thus he acknowledged with thankfulness God's kindness to him in making him that gracious visit and promise: and thus he testified his confidence in, and dependence upon the word which God had spoken. (2.) As his constant practice, whithersoever he removed. As soon as Abram was got to Canaan, though he was but a stranger and sojourner there, yet he set up, and kept up, the worship of God in his family; and wherever he had a tent, God had an altar and that an altar sanctified by prayer.

glossa.text:
« Go out of the land, » etc. ((AUG. ubi supra.)) The narrative of Stephen on this matter is to be considered, etc., *as far as* thus therefore Abram was settled in that land, when he lived there until the birth of Jacob.

((STRAB.)) It is to be noted that he had already gone out of his own land, but had then gone out in body, not in mind and will; for he had perhaps a mind of returning, when it was said to him: « Go out, » etc.

((ISID.)) Christ left the land and the kindred of the Jews, and was magnified among the peoples of the Gentiles. We too must go out of our land, that is, out of earthly means and riches, and out of our kindred, that is, the converse of the vices, which, cleaving to us from our birth, are joined to us as it were by the affinities of blood; and « out of the house of our father, » that is, out of the memory of the world, that renouncing it we may be enlarged with the people of God, and, when the time shall come, be brought into the land of the heavenly promise.

And I will make thee into a great nation, » etc. ((ISID.)) Two things are promised to Abraham, namely, that his seed shall possess the land of Chanaan, when it is said: « And come into the land which I shall show thee. » But the other far more excellent, not of carnal but of spiritual seed, whereof he is to be the father, not only of the Jewish nation, but of all the Gentiles that follow his faith; which is thus promised: « And in thee shall all the nations of the earth be blessed. »
« Seventy-five years old. » ((HIERON. in Q. Hebr.)) If Thare, the father of Abraham, in the Chaldean region, etc., *as far as* and tarried there a longer while.

« Bethel. » ((RAB.)) It is interpreted *the house of God,* which afterwards was called Bethaven, that is, *the house of an idol.*

« Hai. » *Mystically.* Hai is interpreted *eye* or *fountain*. The patriarch therefore, making for the land of promise, pitched his tent between Bethel and Hai, because the saints, regenerated by the font of baptism, circumspect in the course of this life, hasten to the tabernacle of God, that is, to the heavenly city.

notes.text: Harp, &c. — These instruments were used in the publick worship of God in the tabernacle.
A new song — Renewed or continued from day to day.
The word — All God's counsels and commands are wise, and just, and good. His works - All his works of providence agree with his word, and are the accomplishment of his promises or threatenings.
Goodness — He not only doth no man wrong, but he is kind and merciful to all men.
The word — God made this admirable structure of the heavens, and all its glorious stars; not with great pains and time, but with one single word. Host - The angels: or the stars.
Store-houses — Either in the clouds, or in the bowels of the earth.

The Lord — Thus he passes from the work of creation, to the works of providence, and from the instances of his power, in senseless and irrational creatures, to his power in over-ruling the thoughts and wills, and actions of men, whether single or united.
The Counsel — All his purposes and designs are always successful.

glossa.text: *Exult ye,* etc. ((AUG.)) The crooked man praises God when it is well with him; he blasphemes when it is ill: the upright man always, like Job.

*On the harp.* ((ID.)) It sounds from below, and is of the earth, whence we may praise, that is, prosperity and adversity, which are ours from him. *On the psaltery.* When thou attendest to the higher things which he has given thee, the heavenly doctrine. By *the harp* the flesh is understood, by *the psaltery* charity: to which the ten precepts of the law belong: three in the first table toward God, seven in the second toward the neighbour.

*Sing ye to him,* etc. As if to say, what more shall I say? Be glad especially over the incarnation. *A new canticle.* ((CASS.)) Because it does not suffice, unless your justice abound more than that of the Scribes and Pharisees ((Matth. V)).

*Sing ye a new canticle.* Of the incarnation, over which the world exults, of which the Angels sang.

*For it is right.* He has set out the manner of praise: now, why is he to be praised? *And all his works.* ((AUG.)) Lest anyone think that he has come to faith by merits, since in faith are all the works which God loves, that is, rewards, ((ID.)) because he does not work save in the faithful; whence: *Thy faith hath made thee whole ((Matth. X))*. Or, all works are right, etc., *as far as* because he remains wicked, and the more wicked for this, that he sees the just man favour him.

*In faith.* As if in outward things, if a man has been faithful for the sake of justice, He will add inward faith, whom not knowing he feared; whence: who will not give him the things that are his own, who was faithful in another's? ((AUG.)) God is faithful in giving to man what he promised: man is faithful in believing him that promises, and by the promise God is our debtor.
*The earth.* ((ID.)) The Church everywhere upon the earth.

*By the word.* That is, by the wisdom of God the Father. *The heavens.* The Apostles were fully instructed, by conversing with him even bodily: and afterward *all their power,* once had, was strengthened by the Spirit of the Son, through the heavens made firm he gathers and consolidates men into the unity of faith, hope and charity. *The bottle,* the Church, in which is dead flesh. *Even the depths,* that is, those deep in the darkness of vices, he sets among those who are a treasure, whence wisdom enriches others. ((AUG.)) *The earth.* The heavens do not need mercy, etc., *as far as* which he works. *Their power.* Since they were among wolves, etc., *as far as* licence.

*As in a bottle.* ((CASS.)) According to the letter: as he shuts in the sea by its shores, so he shuts within the Church the wavering peoples; and in the treasures of his wisdom he places the deep heights, that he may prove who searches the Scriptures with a zeal for godliness.

*Let all the earth fear.* ((ID.)) The Church out of the sea, etc., *as far as* but let the earth fear the Lord. Let it fear — nay rather, let them be moved by the hand of mercy out of the likeness of one asleep. *By him,* because he himself created it: and therefore he governs it profitably, because something is moved by the devil also, but what is moved by God is moved profitably, therefore *by him. Let them be moved.* ((AUG.)) Not by the terrors of men, etc., *as far as* power not save from God.
*He spoke and they were made.* He notes creation and formation together. He commanded the re-creation.

*He scatters the counsels.* ((CASS.)) That the counsels against himself, as those of the Jews, and against his own, may have no effect. *Of the Gentiles.* When he destroyed idolatry. *Of the peoples.* Of the Jews, whose will, though fulfilled, was yet reproved by the resurrection. *Of the princes.* Of tyrants or of demons.

*But the counsel of the Lord,* etc. ((ID.)) The secret of the incarnation, in which he took counsel for man.

*Standeth for ever.* Because it is unto the obtaining of eternal salvation for us.

*The thoughts.* Predestination, in which all things are laid up, which also so abide as they were foreseen.

*Blessed is the nation.* ((CASS.)) He calls him blessed who has come to the worship of God: which happens in Christian times, in which the Gentiles are converted, these are the just and the upright whom praise becomes. ((AUG.)) All blessedness is in the mind, etc., *as far as* blessed is the people that has God for its possessor.

notes.text: The promise, that he should be the heir of the world — Is the same as that he should be "the father of all nations," namely, of those in all nations who receive the blessing. The whole world was promised to him and them conjointly. Christ is the heir of the world, and of all things; and so are all Abraham's seed, all that believe in him with the faith of Abraham
If they only who are of the law — Who have kept the whole law. Are heirs, faith is made void - No blessing being to be obtained by it; and so the promise is of no effect.

Because the law — Considered apart from that grace, which though it was in fact mingled with it, yet is no part of the legal dispensation, is so difficult, and we so weak and sinful, that, instead of bringing us a blessing, it only worketh wrath; it becomes to us an occasion of wrath, and exposes us to punishment as transgressors. Where there is no law in force, there can be no transgression of it.

Therefore it — The blessing. Is of faith, that it might be of grace - That it might appear to flow from the free love of God, and that the promise might be firm, sure, and effectual, to all the spiritual seed of Abraham; not only Jews, but gentiles also, if they follow his faith.

Before God — Though before men nothing of this appeared, those nations being then unborn. As quickening the dead - The dead are not dead to him and even the things that are not, are before God. And calling the things that are not - Summoning them to rise into being, and appear before him. The seed of Abraham did not then exist; yet God said, "So shall thy seed be." A man can say to his servant actually existing, Do this; and he doeth it: but God saith to the light, while it does not exist, Go forth; and it goeth. Gen. xvii, 5. 18-21. The Apostle shows the power and excellence of that faith to which he ascribes justification. Who against hope - Against all probability, believed and hoped in the promise. The same thing is apprehended both by faith and hope; by faith, as a thing which God has spoken; by hope, as a good thing which God has promised to us. So shall thy seed be - Both natural and spiritual, as the stars of heaven for multitude. Gen. xv, 5.
On his account only — To do personal honour to him.

But on ours also — To establish us in seeking justification by faith, and not by works; and to afford a full answer to those who say that, " to be justified by works means only, by Judaism; to be justified by faith means, by embracing Christianity, that is, the system of doctrines so called." Sure it is that Abraham could not in this sense be justified either by faith or by works; and equally sure that David (taking the words thus) was justified by works, and not by faith. Who raised up Jesus from the dead - As he did in a manner both Abraham and Sarah. If we believe on him who raised up Jesus - God the Father therefore is the proper object of justifying faith. It is observable, that St. Paul here, in speaking both of our faith and of the faith of Abraham, puts a part for the whole. And he mentions that part, with regard to Abraham, which would naturally affect the Jews most.
Who was delivered — To death. For our offenses - As an atonement for them. And raised for our justification - To empower us to receive that atonement by faith.

glossa.text: *For not through the law was the promise.* Other promises were made to Christ than to Abraham. For to Abraham they were made thus, that those who should imitate him in that manner would be blessed by Christ; but to Christ not so, but so that he should not only be the exemplar and form of the ordering of morals and of works, but that he should bless with an eternal blessing those who imitate him. *To his seed.* That is, to all believers who are the seed of Abraham, not by flesh, but by imitation. Or to Christ, to whom the promise is said to have been made, because it was to be fulfilled in him.

*For if,* etc. As if he should say: Truly Abraham is not the heir of the world through the law: because his sons through the law are not those sons who are called heirs, namely as possessing what he himself has. For if this were so, these incongruities would follow from it: that faith would be made void, by which it stands that Abraham was just; that the promise would be abolished, that is, unfulfilled, so that there are no heirs: for the law makes no heirs, since rather it works wrath, and so transgression; for from it comes transgression, because without it there is none. Therefore, because if these things would follow from the law, then it is from faith that they are heirs, and so the promise is firm.

*The law works wrath.* That it might make offenders guilty, not by an efficient cause, but by grace not helping; or it would make them guilty by temporal punishments, it would work wrath, because [it works] transgression; and in what manner this is, he opens, saying:

*For where,* etc. ((ORIG.)) He shows that there cannot be transgression unless there has been a law; yet not that, if there is a law, there will in every kind be transgression: for it can come about that there is a law and there is no transgression, but not conversely.

*Nor transgression.* He does not say: There is no iniquity. For everyone who passes the law by is unjust, but not the contrary. For those who have not received the law can be called unjust, but they cannot be called transgressors.

*Not to him who is of the law.* Because such a man as this has fallen away from grace, and therefore for the sake of faith one must withdraw from the law, that the promise may be firm: for the law, without the grace of the promise, not only does not take away sin, but even increases it.

*Who against hope.* He begins to commend the faith of Abraham, that we may imitate him who through faith received justice and such a promise.

*So shall thy seed be,* etc. It must be known that Abraham first knew God as three and one, and through this merit of faith he obtained the remission of all sins. But after justice, he received a promise from God that he should become the father of many nations. Then again a promise was made to him that his seed should become as the stars, etc.
*He was not weakened.* Some, puffed up by the reasoning of the world, neglected God: therefore the things that are impossible to the world God did, that believing through these they might be saved.

*In the promise.* Isaac, promised against the nature of human generation, was for a sign that the Son of God was to be born of man against human nature; and that the sons of men, through the spirit of regeneration, were to be begotten out of sinners into sons of God, out of mortals into immortals.

*In him who raised up Jesus,* etc. He has fitly entered upon the discourse concerning the Lord, and says: he died not for his own sins, for in that manner he ought not to have risen again, just as neither did any man before him, but for our sins, that he might free us from them. In the same way as he also restored Abraham and the womb of Sarah, already dead through old age and barrenness, to life and to the procreation of children.

*Who was delivered up.* The death of Christ alone signifies the destruction of the old life, and in the resurrection alone is the new life signified, which begins from justification and will be perfected in immortality.

notes.text: He saw a man named Matthew — Modestly so called by himself. The other evangelists call him by his more honourable name, Levi. Sitting - In the very height of his business, at the receipt of custom - The custom house, or place where the customs were received. Mark ii, 14; Luke v, 27.

As Jesus sat at table in the house — Of Matthew, who having invited many of his old companions, made him a feast, Mark ii, 15; and that a great one, though he does not himself mention it. The publicans, or collectors of the taxes which the Jews paid the Romans, were infamous for their illegal exactions: Sinners - Open, notorious, sinners.
The Pharisees said to his disciples, Why eateth your Master? — Thus they commonly ask our Lord, Why do thy disciples this? And his disciples, Why doth your Master?

Go ye and learn — Ye that take upon you to teach others. I will have mercy and not sacrifice - That is, I will have mercy rather than sacrifice. I love acts of mercy better than sacrifice itself. Hosea vi, 6.

glossa.text: *He saw a man.* Here it seems more probable that he is recording things passed over, since he chose the twelve before the sermon. *In the custom-house.* Τέλος in Greek, in Latin a toll. Matthew in Hebrew is in Latin "given", who received so great a gift of grace: Levi, "added" or "taken up", because the divine election took him up and added him to the number of the apostles. *Matthew.* The other Evangelists, out of modesty, etc., *as far as* the aforesaid discourse was. *Rising up. ((BED.))* Luke says more fully: leaving all things, he followed him as much in body as in mind. Led not by levity, but drawn by the truth of the works and by the divine power working within, a perfect obedience and a perfect renunciation, he left his gains also, eager to follow Christ.

*In the house.* He does not say whose, but Luke expresses it, etc., *as far as* is shown by the conversion of the penitent. *Behold many publicans.* A good omen: already by his example many are converted. Already he draws many after him, being about to be an Apostle and teacher of the Gentiles. *((HIER.)) With publicans and sinners.* Tertullian says these were heathen, etc., *as far as* he commanded: *Go ye not into the way of the Gentiles. Sinners coming sat down.* Penitents, by Matthew's example, hoping for pardon: whence Mark says here: *that many followed him ((Marc. II))*.
*Why with publicans.* Every question, etc., *as far as* and all that he did serves for salvation.

*But Jesus hearing it, said.* He both strengthens further in faith the penitents he has received, and provokes the proud to the grace of humility and of mercy. *They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill.* Christ is the physician, etc., *as far as* they receive the word of God, they cannot hunger.

*And going, say ye.* To those swelling with a false righteousness he gives counsel of correction, etc., *as far as* by the sheep, and the drachma, and the two sons. *For I am not come to call the just.* Were not Nathanael, and Peter, and Andrew, etc., *as far as* they no longer seem just to themselves.

echoes.text: I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.”
echoes.note: 'The promise to Abraham and to his seed that he should be heir of the world' (4:13) universalizes the land-inheritance promises of Genesis (17:8 'I will give to you and your offspring... all the land of Canaan for an everlasting possession'; cf. 13:15; 15:7). Paul expands the territorial 'land' to 'the world' (kosmos), a move grounded in the cosmic scope of the promise.

echoes.text: that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your seed greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your seed will possess the gate of his enemies. All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your seed, because you have obeyed my voice.”
echoes.note: The promise to Abraham 'and to his seed' (4:13) echoes the oath of Genesis 22:17-18, 'I will multiply your seed... and in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed,' which links seed, multiplication, and universal blessing — the basis for 'heir of the world.' The word 'seed' (sperma) is the Genesis catchword Paul foregrounds.

echoes.text: Therefore he assured him by an oath, That the nations should be blessed in his seed; That he would multiply him as the dust of the earth, And exalt his seed as the stars, And cause them to inherit from sea to sea, And from the River to the utmost part of the earth.
echoes.note: The 'heir of the world' expansion has a Second Temple precedent in Sirach 44:21, where God promises Abraham 'to give them an inheritance from sea to sea and from the River to the ends of the earth' — already enlarging the land to global scope. A contested background echo for Paul's kosmos language.

echoes.text: He said to him, “I am Yahweh who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give you this land to inherit it.”
echoes.note: Genesis 15:7 ('I am the Lord who brought you out... to give you this land to inherit it'), within the same chapter as 15:6, supplies the inheritance vocabulary Paul universalizes in 'heir of the world.' Faint; reinforces that Paul reads the whole Genesis 15 unit.

echoes.text: Neither will your name any more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.
echoes.note: Quoted verbatim with the introductory formula 'As it is written' in 4:17: 'I have made you a father of many nations' (Genesis 17:5 LXX, 'patera pollon ethnon tetheika se'). Paul reads the perfect tense ('I HAVE made') as already-accomplished divine speech that calls the not-yet into being.

echoes.text: Yahweh brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So will your seed be.”
echoes.note: Quoted verbatim in 4:18: 'So will your seed be' (Genesis 15:5 LXX, 'houtos estai to sperma sou'), the star-promise spoken immediately before Genesis 15:6. Paul binds the two halves of Genesis 15 together: the promise (v.5) and Abraham's believing response reckoned as righteousness (v.6).

echoes.text: Then Abraham fell on his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, “Will a child be born to him who is one hundred years old? Will Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?”
echoes.note: 'He being about a hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah's womb' (4:19) draws directly on Genesis 17:17, where Abraham, told he will have a son, says 'Shall a child be born to him who is a hundred years old? And shall Sarah, who is ninety, bear?' Paul reuses the numeric detail and the implied biological impossibility.

echoes.text: Now Abraham and Sarah were old, well advanced in age. Sarah had passed the age of childbearing. Sarah laughed within herself, saying, “After I have grown old will I have pleasure, my lord being old also?”
echoes.note: 'The deadness of Sarah's womb' and Abraham's 'body already worn out' (4:19) echo Genesis 18:11-12: 'it had ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women,' and Sarah's words 'After I am worn out (LXX katetribe), shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?' Paul's 'worn out' (nenekromenon/already dead) language tracks the Genesis 18 description of both spouses' exhaustion.

echoes.text: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.
echoes.note: The pericope closes in 4:22 by re-quoting the governing text: 'Therefore it also was reckoned to him for righteousness.' Recurrence of Genesis 15:6 as the inclusio binding the demonstration of Abraham's faith back to its scriptural anchor.

echoes.text: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”
echoes.note: Abraham 'being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform' (4:21) answers the rhetorical question of Genesis 18:14, 'Is anything too hard for the Lord? At the appointed time I will return... and Sarah shall have a son.' Paul converts the LORD's question into Abraham's confident assent — God's power over the impossible.

echoes.text: “Yahweh kills, and makes alive. He brings down to Sheol, and brings up.
echoes.note: 'God, who gives life to the dead' (4:17) draws on the scriptural confession of God as life-giver, e.g. 1 Samuel 2:6 (Hannah), 'The Lord kills and makes alive; he brings down to Sheol and raises up.' This is the standard OT idiom Paul applies to both Isaac's miraculous conception and the resurrection.

echoes.text: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.
echoes.note: 'God, who gives life to the dead' (4:17) also resonates with Deuteronomy 32:39, 'I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal,' a foundational text for God's sole power over death and life. Reinforces the same divine attribute Paul predicates.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]
echoes.note: 'God, who gives life to the dead' (4:17) may figurally echo Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, where the Spirit raises a dead Israel to life — a paradigm of resurrection-as-restoration. Thematically coherent with Paul's resurrection horizon; verbally faint, marked contested.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters. God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
echoes.note: 'Calls the things that are not, as though they were' (4:17) figurally echoes the creation account, where God's word summons being out of nonbeing ('Let there be... and there was'). Paul pairs creation (calling the nonexistent) with resurrection (giving life to the dead) as twin marks of the God Abraham believed.

echoes.text: I beseech you, my child, to lift your eyes to the heaven and the earth, and to see all things that are therein, and thus to recognize that God made them not of things that were, and that the race of men in this wise comes into being.
echoes.note: 'Calls the things that are not, as though they were' (4:17) has its closest Second Temple parallel in 2 Maccabees 7:28, where the mother urges her son to recognize 'that God did not make them out of things that existed' — an early articulation of creation from nothing, paired (as in Romans 4) with resurrection hope. Contested background echo.

echoes.text: Yes, my hand has laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand has spread out the heavens: when I call to them, they stand up together.
echoes.note: 'Calls the things that are not, as though they were' (4:17) may echo the Isaianic creator who 'calls' the heavens and earth into existence (Isaiah 48:13; 41:4; 44:24), where divine calling is creative summons. Faint verbal link via the verb 'call'; marked contested.

echoes.text: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.
echoes.note: 'Now it was not written that it was accounted to him for his sake alone, but for our sake also, to whom it will be accounted' (4:23-24) explicitly thematizes the act of reading Genesis 15:6 as Scripture written for the church. The verb 'accounted/reckoned' is carried forward one last time, applied now to believers in the God who raised Jesus.

echoes.text: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'Who was delivered up for our trespasses' (4:25) echoes Isaiah 53 LXX, especially 53:6 ('the Lord delivered him up for our sins,' paredoken auton tais hamartiais hemon) and 53:12 ('he was delivered up because of their sins'). Paul's verb 'delivered up' (paredothe) plus 'for our trespasses' is verbatim Servant-song language, identifying the crucified Jesus as the suffering Servant.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'And was raised for our justification' (4:25) draws on Isaiah 53:11 LXX, 'the righteous one will justify the many (dikaiosai dikaion... tois pollois), and he shall bear their sins.' The pairing of the Servant's vindication with the justification 'of many' undergirds Paul's resurrection-justification clause, linking the Abraham-righteousness midrash to the Servant's righteousness.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: Formula-marked citation, 'go and learn what this means: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.' Verbatim from Hosea (LXX eleos ou thysian). Jesus deploys the prophetic preference for covenant loyalty over cultic act to justify table fellowship with sinners; Matthew alone repeats it at 12:7.

echoes.text: Samuel said, “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of Yahweh? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.
echoes.note: 'To obey is better than sacrifice.' Samuel's rebuke of Saul belongs to the same prophetic tradition prioritizing obedience/mercy over cult that Hosea 6:6 distills; it reinforces the scriptural logic Jesus wields against the Pharisees.

echoes.text: To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to Yahweh than sacrifice.
echoes.note: 'To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.' A wisdom parallel to Hosea 6:6 corroborating the mercy-over-sacrifice principle invoked to defend eating with tax collectors.

echoes.text: Honor a physician according to your need of him with the honors due to him: For verily the Lord has created him. For from the Most High comes healing; And from the king he shall receive a gift. The skill of the physician shall lift up his head; And in the sight of great men he shall be admired. The Lord created medicines out of the earth; And a prudent man will have no disgust at them.
echoes.note: 'Honor the physician... the Lord created medicines.' Jesus' aphorism 'those who are sick need a physician' uses the physician topos; Sirach's Second Temple esteem for the healer is a contemporary backdrop, though the saying is proverbial rather than a specific borrowing.

echoes.text: I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but the fat and the strong I will destroy; I will feed them in justice.
echoes.note: 'I will seek the lost... and bind up the injured.' The shepherd-God who goes after the sick and strayed anticipates Jesus' coming 'not to call the righteous but sinners,' the same pastoral logic, faintly heard here and developed at 9:36.

doctrine.title: Articles of Religion
doctrine.article: Art. IX, the Justification of Man

notes.text: Come — The prophet here brings them in, exhorting one another. He hath torn - We now see his hand in all we suffer.

After two days — After some short time of suffering, God will shew us his favour, and revive our dead state. Revive us - Though we were as dead men, buried in our miseries, yet our merciful God will quicken us. Live - Flourish in peace, wealth, and joy; in righteousness and safety. In his sight - The eye of our God being upon us for good.

Know — What worship he requires. And the knowledge of God shall be to us a spring of all holy, righteous, sober conversation. Follow on - By a diligent attendance to the word, and works of God, we shall know experimentally, how holy, how good, how faithful God is. His going forth - Before his people; his gracious, faithful, holy, just, and wise providence, for his peoples good and comfort. As the morning - As sure, beautiful, grateful, and as clear as the morning; which dispels the darkness, and proclaims its own approach. As the rain - Which revives, makes it fruitful, beautifies it, and gives a new face to all.
What shall I do — What shall I do more to save you from ruin, and save my own honour, truth, and justice?

Therefore — Because I would do for you whatever might be done. Hewed them - I have severely, and unweariedly reproved, and threatened them. By thy words - As I did by word foretel, so I did effect in due time. Thy judgments - The punishments threatened, which fell upon this people, did so fully answer the prediction that every one might see them clear as the light, and as constantly executed as the morning.

For — I so hewed and slew them, because they did not what I most of all required; they were full of sacrifices, but either to idols, or else in formality and pride. Mercy - Compassion and charity towards men, this one principal duty of the second table put for all. In this I delight, I have found little of this among you. Not sacrifice - Rather than sacrifice. The knowledge of God - The affectionate knowledge of God, which fills the mind with reverence of his majesty, fear of his goodness, love of his holiness, trust in his promise, and submission to his will.

Hear — Having brought in God, as coming to judgment, he now gives an account of the process and sentence of the judge. Testify - I will declare my charge against thee. Thy God - Not only in general, but in a special manner, by that solemn covenant made at Sinai; whereby I avouched thee to be my peculiar people, and thou didst avouch me to be thy God.
I will not — This is not the principal matter of my charge, that thou hast neglected sacrifices which thou shouldst have offered.
Bullock — Be not so foolish, as to imagine that thou dost lay any obligations upon me by thy sacrifices.
The fowls — Such as are wild and fly up and down upon mountains.

Offer — If thou wouldest know what sacrifices I prize, and indispensably require, in the first place, it is that of thankfulness, proportionable to my great and numberless favours; which doth not consist barely in verbal acknowledgments, but proceeds from an heart deeply affected with God's mercies, and is accompanied with such a course of life, as is well-pleasing to God. Vows - Those substantial vows and promises, which were the very soul of their sacrifices.

Call — And make conscience of that great duty of fervent prayer, which is an acknowledgment of thy subjection to me, and of thy trust and dependance upon me. Glorify - Thou shalt have occasion to glorify me for thy deliverance.

glossa.text:
*Hear, O my people, etc.* ((CASS.)) The voice of Christ, that, the sacrifices of cattle being left, there may be made a sacrifice of praise. ((AUG.)) Or, he repeats under another word, Hear as Israel, that is, as one seeing God, and *I will testify,* these things, namely, *I am thy God.*

*Thy God.* ((AUG.)) First he says simply: *I am God.* And afterwards he says: *I am thy God.* As if he should say: Even if I am not thy God, yet I am God. For to my own good I am God, but to thy evil I am not thy God. *I am.* ((CASS.)) To be is proper to the Deity. *Hear, O Israel. ((Ibid.))* As if he should say: If thou art Israel, that is, if thou seest me, thou dost not neglect to hear. That God is general, thy God properly.

*But the holocausts.* ((AUG.)) If the soul is inflamed, and seizes the members into its own use, that they may not serve concupiscence: whence it is commanded in Leviticus, that they offer the fat with the little kidneys, by which the inward charity is signified.

*I will not take,* etc. ((CASS.)) Even if thou shalt so do: *I will not take calves out of thy house,* as though I took the things signified, not those out of the house. *For mine are:* as if he should say, because they are not thine, but mine. *For mine are,* etc. ((AUG.)) Mine are the things which thou dost not possess, the untamed, namely: *The beasts of the woods, the cattle, the oxen,* etc. ((CASS.)) By these likenesses he figures the Church, etc., *as far as: The flesh of bullocks* he wills not in sacrifices, but in the poor.

VERS, 11.-- *I know all the fowls.* ((AUG.)) With him are all things, by a certain knowledge of ineffable wisdom.
*If I should be hungry, I would not. ((Ibid.))* If you give these things, perhaps you think that I hunger, which is madness?

*Shall I eat the flesh of bullocks?* Of old these things were sacrificed, not for this reason that God was delighted therein, but lest they should be offered to demons, and they were sacrificed to God only, in which there was some signification.

*Sacrifice to God.* ((CASS.)) He says not "to me," but of himself, as of another, as also afterwards: *But to the sinner God hath said, not I.*
*Of tribulation.* ((AUG.)) Our tribulation is properly by the fear of salvation, not of carnal things.

notes.text: The promise, that he should be the heir of the world — Is the same as that he should be "the father of all nations," namely, of those in all nations who receive the blessing. The whole world was promised to him and them conjointly. Christ is the heir of the world, and of all things; and so are all Abraham's seed, all that believe in him with the faith of Abraham
If they only who are of the law — Who have kept the whole law. Are heirs, faith is made void - No blessing being to be obtained by it; and so the promise is of no effect.

Because the law — Considered apart from that grace, which though it was in fact mingled with it, yet is no part of the legal dispensation, is so difficult, and we so weak and sinful, that, instead of bringing us a blessing, it only worketh wrath; it becomes to us an occasion of wrath, and exposes us to punishment as transgressors. Where there is no law in force, there can be no transgression of it.

Therefore it — The blessing. Is of faith, that it might be of grace - That it might appear to flow from the free love of God, and that the promise might be firm, sure, and effectual, to all the spiritual seed of Abraham; not only Jews, but gentiles also, if they follow his faith.

Before God — Though before men nothing of this appeared, those nations being then unborn. As quickening the dead - The dead are not dead to him and even the things that are not, are before God. And calling the things that are not - Summoning them to rise into being, and appear before him. The seed of Abraham did not then exist; yet God said, "So shall thy seed be." A man can say to his servant actually existing, Do this; and he doeth it: but God saith to the light, while it does not exist, Go forth; and it goeth. Gen. xvii, 5. 18-21. The Apostle shows the power and excellence of that faith to which he ascribes justification. Who against hope - Against all probability, believed and hoped in the promise. The same thing is apprehended both by faith and hope; by faith, as a thing which God has spoken; by hope, as a good thing which God has promised to us. So shall thy seed be - Both natural and spiritual, as the stars of heaven for multitude. Gen. xv, 5.
On his account only — To do personal honour to him.

But on ours also — To establish us in seeking justification by faith, and not by works; and to afford a full answer to those who say that, " to be justified by works means only, by Judaism; to be justified by faith means, by embracing Christianity, that is, the system of doctrines so called." Sure it is that Abraham could not in this sense be justified either by faith or by works; and equally sure that David (taking the words thus) was justified by works, and not by faith. Who raised up Jesus from the dead - As he did in a manner both Abraham and Sarah. If we believe on him who raised up Jesus - God the Father therefore is the proper object of justifying faith. It is observable, that St. Paul here, in speaking both of our faith and of the faith of Abraham, puts a part for the whole. And he mentions that part, with regard to Abraham, which would naturally affect the Jews most.
Who was delivered — To death. For our offenses - As an atonement for them. And raised for our justification - To empower us to receive that atonement by faith.

glossa.text: *For not through the law was the promise.* Other promises were made to Christ than to Abraham. For to Abraham they were made thus, that those who should imitate him in that manner would be blessed by Christ; but to Christ not so, but so that he should not only be the exemplar and form of the ordering of morals and of works, but that he should bless with an eternal blessing those who imitate him. *To his seed.* That is, to all believers who are the seed of Abraham, not by flesh, but by imitation. Or to Christ, to whom the promise is said to have been made, because it was to be fulfilled in him.

*For if,* etc. As if he should say: Truly Abraham is not the heir of the world through the law: because his sons through the law are not those sons who are called heirs, namely as possessing what he himself has. For if this were so, these incongruities would follow from it: that faith would be made void, by which it stands that Abraham was just; that the promise would be abolished, that is, unfulfilled, so that there are no heirs: for the law makes no heirs, since rather it works wrath, and so transgression; for from it comes transgression, because without it there is none. Therefore, because if these things would follow from the law, then it is from faith that they are heirs, and so the promise is firm.

*The law works wrath.* That it might make offenders guilty, not by an efficient cause, but by grace not helping; or it would make them guilty by temporal punishments, it would work wrath, because [it works] transgression; and in what manner this is, he opens, saying:

*For where,* etc. ((ORIG.)) He shows that there cannot be transgression unless there has been a law; yet not that, if there is a law, there will in every kind be transgression: for it can come about that there is a law and there is no transgression, but not conversely.

*Nor transgression.* He does not say: There is no iniquity. For everyone who passes the law by is unjust, but not the contrary. For those who have not received the law can be called unjust, but they cannot be called transgressors.

*Not to him who is of the law.* Because such a man as this has fallen away from grace, and therefore for the sake of faith one must withdraw from the law, that the promise may be firm: for the law, without the grace of the promise, not only does not take away sin, but even increases it.

*Who against hope.* He begins to commend the faith of Abraham, that we may imitate him who through faith received justice and such a promise.

*So shall thy seed be,* etc. It must be known that Abraham first knew God as three and one, and through this merit of faith he obtained the remission of all sins. But after justice, he received a promise from God that he should become the father of many nations. Then again a promise was made to him that his seed should become as the stars, etc.
*He was not weakened.* Some, puffed up by the reasoning of the world, neglected God: therefore the things that are impossible to the world God did, that believing through these they might be saved.

*In the promise.* Isaac, promised against the nature of human generation, was for a sign that the Son of God was to be born of man against human nature; and that the sons of men, through the spirit of regeneration, were to be begotten out of sinners into sons of God, out of mortals into immortals.

*In him who raised up Jesus,* etc. He has fitly entered upon the discourse concerning the Lord, and says: he died not for his own sins, for in that manner he ought not to have risen again, just as neither did any man before him, but for our sins, that he might free us from them. In the same way as he also restored Abraham and the womb of Sarah, already dead through old age and barrenness, to life and to the procreation of children.

*Who was delivered up.* The death of Christ alone signifies the destruction of the old life, and in the resurrection alone is the new life signified, which begins from justification and will be perfected in immortality.

notes.text: He saw a man named Matthew — Modestly so called by himself. The other evangelists call him by his more honourable name, Levi. Sitting - In the very height of his business, at the receipt of custom - The custom house, or place where the customs were received. Mark ii, 14; Luke v, 27.

As Jesus sat at table in the house — Of Matthew, who having invited many of his old companions, made him a feast, Mark ii, 15; and that a great one, though he does not himself mention it. The publicans, or collectors of the taxes which the Jews paid the Romans, were infamous for their illegal exactions: Sinners - Open, notorious, sinners.
The Pharisees said to his disciples, Why eateth your Master? — Thus they commonly ask our Lord, Why do thy disciples this? And his disciples, Why doth your Master?

Go ye and learn — Ye that take upon you to teach others. I will have mercy and not sacrifice - That is, I will have mercy rather than sacrifice. I love acts of mercy better than sacrifice itself. Hosea vi, 6.

glossa.text: *He saw a man.* Here it seems more probable that he is recording things passed over, since he chose the twelve before the sermon. *In the custom-house.* Τέλος in Greek, in Latin a toll. Matthew in Hebrew is in Latin "given", who received so great a gift of grace: Levi, "added" or "taken up", because the divine election took him up and added him to the number of the apostles. *Matthew.* The other Evangelists, out of modesty, etc., *as far as* the aforesaid discourse was. *Rising up. ((BED.))* Luke says more fully: leaving all things, he followed him as much in body as in mind. Led not by levity, but drawn by the truth of the works and by the divine power working within, a perfect obedience and a perfect renunciation, he left his gains also, eager to follow Christ.

*In the house.* He does not say whose, but Luke expresses it, etc., *as far as* is shown by the conversion of the penitent. *Behold many publicans.* A good omen: already by his example many are converted. Already he draws many after him, being about to be an Apostle and teacher of the Gentiles. *((HIER.)) With publicans and sinners.* Tertullian says these were heathen, etc., *as far as* he commanded: *Go ye not into the way of the Gentiles. Sinners coming sat down.* Penitents, by Matthew's example, hoping for pardon: whence Mark says here: *that many followed him ((Marc. II))*.
*Why with publicans.* Every question, etc., *as far as* and all that he did serves for salvation.

*But Jesus hearing it, said.* He both strengthens further in faith the penitents he has received, and provokes the proud to the grace of humility and of mercy. *They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill.* Christ is the physician, etc., *as far as* they receive the word of God, they cannot hunger.

*And going, say ye.* To those swelling with a false righteousness he gives counsel of correction, etc., *as far as* by the sheep, and the drachma, and the two sons. *For I am not come to call the just.* Were not Nathanael, and Peter, and Andrew, etc., *as far as* they no longer seem just to themselves.

Come to the table of mercy
Come, sinners, to the gospel feast
Come, sinners to the gospel feast
Come, ye sinners, poor and needy
Be present at our table, Lord

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: I will give to you, and to your seed after you, the land where you are traveling, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession. I will be their God.”
echoes.note: 'The promise to Abraham and to his seed that he should be heir of the world' (4:13) universalizes the land-inheritance promises of Genesis (17:8 'I will give to you and your offspring... all the land of Canaan for an everlasting possession'; cf. 13:15; 15:7). Paul expands the territorial 'land' to 'the world' (kosmos), a move grounded in the cosmic scope of the promise.

echoes.text: that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your seed greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your seed will possess the gate of his enemies. All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your seed, because you have obeyed my voice.”
echoes.note: The promise to Abraham 'and to his seed' (4:13) echoes the oath of Genesis 22:17-18, 'I will multiply your seed... and in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed,' which links seed, multiplication, and universal blessing — the basis for 'heir of the world.' The word 'seed' (sperma) is the Genesis catchword Paul foregrounds.

echoes.text: Therefore he assured him by an oath, That the nations should be blessed in his seed; That he would multiply him as the dust of the earth, And exalt his seed as the stars, And cause them to inherit from sea to sea, And from the River to the utmost part of the earth.
echoes.note: The 'heir of the world' expansion has a Second Temple precedent in Sirach 44:21, where God promises Abraham 'to give them an inheritance from sea to sea and from the River to the ends of the earth' — already enlarging the land to global scope. A contested background echo for Paul's kosmos language.

echoes.text: He said to him, “I am Yahweh who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give you this land to inherit it.”
echoes.note: Genesis 15:7 ('I am the Lord who brought you out... to give you this land to inherit it'), within the same chapter as 15:6, supplies the inheritance vocabulary Paul universalizes in 'heir of the world.' Faint; reinforces that Paul reads the whole Genesis 15 unit.

echoes.text: Neither will your name any more be called Abram, but your name will be Abraham; for I have made you the father of a multitude of nations.
echoes.note: Quoted verbatim with the introductory formula 'As it is written' in 4:17: 'I have made you a father of many nations' (Genesis 17:5 LXX, 'patera pollon ethnon tetheika se'). Paul reads the perfect tense ('I HAVE made') as already-accomplished divine speech that calls the not-yet into being.

echoes.text: Yahweh brought him outside, and said, “Look now toward the sky, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” He said to Abram, “So will your seed be.”
echoes.note: Quoted verbatim in 4:18: 'So will your seed be' (Genesis 15:5 LXX, 'houtos estai to sperma sou'), the star-promise spoken immediately before Genesis 15:6. Paul binds the two halves of Genesis 15 together: the promise (v.5) and Abraham's believing response reckoned as righteousness (v.6).

echoes.text: Then Abraham fell on his face, and laughed, and said in his heart, “Will a child be born to him who is one hundred years old? Will Sarah, who is ninety years old, give birth?”
echoes.note: 'He being about a hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah's womb' (4:19) draws directly on Genesis 17:17, where Abraham, told he will have a son, says 'Shall a child be born to him who is a hundred years old? And shall Sarah, who is ninety, bear?' Paul reuses the numeric detail and the implied biological impossibility.

echoes.text: Now Abraham and Sarah were old, well advanced in age. Sarah had passed the age of childbearing. Sarah laughed within herself, saying, “After I have grown old will I have pleasure, my lord being old also?”
echoes.note: 'The deadness of Sarah's womb' and Abraham's 'body already worn out' (4:19) echo Genesis 18:11-12: 'it had ceased to be with Sarah after the manner of women,' and Sarah's words 'After I am worn out (LXX katetribe), shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?' Paul's 'worn out' (nenekromenon/already dead) language tracks the Genesis 18 description of both spouses' exhaustion.

echoes.text: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.
echoes.note: The pericope closes in 4:22 by re-quoting the governing text: 'Therefore it also was reckoned to him for righteousness.' Recurrence of Genesis 15:6 as the inclusio binding the demonstration of Abraham's faith back to its scriptural anchor.

echoes.text: Is anything too hard for Yahweh? At the set time I will return to you, when the season comes round, and Sarah will have a son.”
echoes.note: Abraham 'being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform' (4:21) answers the rhetorical question of Genesis 18:14, 'Is anything too hard for the Lord? At the appointed time I will return... and Sarah shall have a son.' Paul converts the LORD's question into Abraham's confident assent — God's power over the impossible.

echoes.text: “Yahweh kills, and makes alive. He brings down to Sheol, and brings up.
echoes.note: 'God, who gives life to the dead' (4:17) draws on the scriptural confession of God as life-giver, e.g. 1 Samuel 2:6 (Hannah), 'The Lord kills and makes alive; he brings down to Sheol and raises up.' This is the standard OT idiom Paul applies to both Isaac's miraculous conception and the resurrection.

echoes.text: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.
echoes.note: 'God, who gives life to the dead' (4:17) also resonates with Deuteronomy 32:39, 'I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal,' a foundational text for God's sole power over death and life. Reinforces the same divine attribute Paul predicates.

echoes.text: The hand of Yahweh was on me, and he brought me out in the Spirit of Yahweh, and set me down in the midst of the valley; and it was full of bones. He caused me to pass by them all around: and behold, there were very many in the open valley; and behold, they were very dry. He said to me, Son of man, can these bones live? I answered, Lord Yahweh, you know. Again he said to me, Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, you dry bones, hear Yahweh’s word. Thus […]
echoes.note: 'God, who gives life to the dead' (4:17) may figurally echo Ezekiel's valley of dry bones, where the Spirit raises a dead Israel to life — a paradigm of resurrection-as-restoration. Thematically coherent with Paul's resurrection horizon; verbally faint, marked contested.

echoes.text: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. The earth was formless and empty. Darkness was on the surface of the deep and God’s Spirit was hovering over the surface of the waters. God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
echoes.note: 'Calls the things that are not, as though they were' (4:17) figurally echoes the creation account, where God's word summons being out of nonbeing ('Let there be... and there was'). Paul pairs creation (calling the nonexistent) with resurrection (giving life to the dead) as twin marks of the God Abraham believed.

echoes.text: I beseech you, my child, to lift your eyes to the heaven and the earth, and to see all things that are therein, and thus to recognize that God made them not of things that were, and that the race of men in this wise comes into being.
echoes.note: 'Calls the things that are not, as though they were' (4:17) has its closest Second Temple parallel in 2 Maccabees 7:28, where the mother urges her son to recognize 'that God did not make them out of things that existed' — an early articulation of creation from nothing, paired (as in Romans 4) with resurrection hope. Contested background echo.

echoes.text: Yes, my hand has laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand has spread out the heavens: when I call to them, they stand up together.
echoes.note: 'Calls the things that are not, as though they were' (4:17) may echo the Isaianic creator who 'calls' the heavens and earth into existence (Isaiah 48:13; 41:4; 44:24), where divine calling is creative summons. Faint verbal link via the verb 'call'; marked contested.

echoes.text: He believed in Yahweh; and he reckoned it to him for righteousness.
echoes.note: 'Now it was not written that it was accounted to him for his sake alone, but for our sake also, to whom it will be accounted' (4:23-24) explicitly thematizes the act of reading Genesis 15:6 as Scripture written for the church. The verb 'accounted/reckoned' is carried forward one last time, applied now to believers in the God who raised Jesus.

echoes.text: But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed. All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
echoes.note: 'Who was delivered up for our trespasses' (4:25) echoes Isaiah 53 LXX, especially 53:6 ('the Lord delivered him up for our sins,' paredoken auton tais hamartiais hemon) and 53:12 ('he was delivered up because of their sins'). Paul's verb 'delivered up' (paredothe) plus 'for our trespasses' is verbatim Servant-song language, identifying the crucified Jesus as the suffering Servant.

echoes.text: After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: 'And was raised for our justification' (4:25) draws on Isaiah 53:11 LXX, 'the righteous one will justify the many (dikaiosai dikaion... tois pollois), and he shall bear their sins.' The pairing of the Servant's vindication with the justification 'of many' undergirds Paul's resurrection-justification clause, linking the Abraham-righteousness midrash to the Servant's righteousness.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: Formula-marked citation, 'go and learn what this means: I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.' Verbatim from Hosea (LXX eleos ou thysian). Jesus deploys the prophetic preference for covenant loyalty over cultic act to justify table fellowship with sinners; Matthew alone repeats it at 12:7.

echoes.text: Samuel said, “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of Yahweh? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.
echoes.note: 'To obey is better than sacrifice.' Samuel's rebuke of Saul belongs to the same prophetic tradition prioritizing obedience/mercy over cult that Hosea 6:6 distills; it reinforces the scriptural logic Jesus wields against the Pharisees.

echoes.text: To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to Yahweh than sacrifice.
echoes.note: 'To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.' A wisdom parallel to Hosea 6:6 corroborating the mercy-over-sacrifice principle invoked to defend eating with tax collectors.

echoes.text: Honor a physician according to your need of him with the honors due to him: For verily the Lord has created him. For from the Most High comes healing; And from the king he shall receive a gift. The skill of the physician shall lift up his head; And in the sight of great men he shall be admired. The Lord created medicines out of the earth; And a prudent man will have no disgust at them.
echoes.note: 'Honor the physician... the Lord created medicines.' Jesus' aphorism 'those who are sick need a physician' uses the physician topos; Sirach's Second Temple esteem for the healer is a contemporary backdrop, though the saying is proverbial rather than a specific borrowing.

echoes.text: I will seek that which was lost, and will bring back that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken, and will strengthen that which was sick: but the fat and the strong I will destroy; I will feed them in justice.
echoes.note: 'I will seek the lost... and bind up the injured.' The shepherd-God who goes after the sick and strayed anticipates Jesus' coming 'not to call the righteous but sinners,' the same pastoral logic, faintly heard here and developed at 9:36.

registers.label: Spare
lines: God said to Abram, Go — and he went.
We have left the familiar to follow.
The road is long, and we cannot see the end.
But the One who calls us keeps the promise.
Jesus passed the tax booth and said, Follow me.
We rose and came, and we are still coming.
Come, let us worship the God who calls.
We come, and we will go where you send us. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Feel the dust of the road still on your feet — you came from somewhere to be here, and God has been with you the whole way.
Here we are; we will follow.
To Abram, settled and old, God said only one word — Go — and a whole new country opened ahead of him.
Here we are; we will follow.
At the tax booth Jesus stopped, looked Matthew in the eye, and said the same word he says to you: come.
Here we are; we will follow.
He sits down to eat with the ones the world wrote off, and there is a place at that table for you.
Here we are; we will follow. Lead on, O God!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: God said to Abram, Go, and the road opened.
Here we are; we will follow.
The dust of the journey is still on our feet.
Here we are; we will follow.
Jesus says, as he said at the tax booth, Follow me.
Here we are; we will follow.
Come, let us worship the God who leads.
Here we are; we will follow. Amen.
